# POWER ANAYLSIS --- RECOMMENDATIONS FOR MONITORING PROGRAM DESIGN/SAMPLING FREQUENCY

We chose a case study of the Hard Bottom Longline Hook Survey to
evaluate sampling design requirements using power analysis to assess how
monitoring programs could be adapted or expanded to detect meaningful
changes in conservation priority species. Power analysis is a widely
used approach for evaluating how sampling design and replication
influence the ability to detect ecological change when it occurs.
Statistical power depends on the magnitude of the effect being tested,
the degree of spatial and temporal variability in indicators, and the
level of replication across sites, years, and sampling units
(Stewart-Oaten et al. 1986; Underwood 1994). In impact monitoring
frameworks such as Before--After--Control--Impact (BACI) designs,
balanced designs with comparable numbers of observations in pre- and
post-impact periods generally provide greater statistical power than
unbalanced designs with the same total sampling effort (Underwood 1994;
Smokorowski and Randall 2017).

The Hard Bottom Longline Survey was selected as an illustrative example
for several reasons. The HBLL was one of the programs that scored
highest in our program assessment based on temporal suitability, domain
relevance, and spatial coverage criteria. It has a 19-year time series
providing sufficient historical data to characterize baseline
variability, monitors multiple MPAN Ecological Conservation Priority
rockfish species (yelloweye, quillback), samples 54 individual protected
areas with coverage both inside and outside MPAN boundaries, and
collects detailed biological data (length, weight, archived otoliths)
enabling analysis of multiple response metrics.

The power analyses conducted on the HBLL were used to inform
recommendations on sampling frequency, spatial replication, and temporal
coverage needed to support robust evaluation of Marine Protected Area
(MPA) performance. Importantly, this case study serves as one
methodological example---not a prescription. The HBLL was not originally
designed for MPA performance assessment; sampling locations were
selected for regional stock assessment. The power analysis demonstrates
what is currently feasible with existing data and what adaptations would
strengthen performance monitoring. Different programs will require
different adaptations depending on their design, species monitored,
spatial scale, logistical constraints, and organizational priorities.
This case study illustrates a general analytical workflow that can be
applied to other high-suitability programs, with final decisions about
program adaptation to be made collaboratively by Network Partners
through the Network Monitoring Strategy process.

## MONITORING PROGRAM DESIGN CONSIDERATIONS

**Statistical robustness in monitoring**

Effective sampling and monitoring design requires statistical
robustness, incorporating careful consideration of sample size,
replication, statistical power, and data independence. Neves et al. (In
prep.) provides comprehensive discussion of factors involved in
monitoring program sampling design, including various sample design
types, BACI approaches, and reference site selection (DFO 2021a).

**Replication**

Establishing appropriate replication levels---whether measured in number
of sites, years, or samples within sites---presents significant
challenges and varies considerably among projects and indicators (Braun
et al. 2019). Power analyses serve as valuable tools for understanding
how replication influences statistical power, defined as the ability to
detect effects when they exist. Statistical power depends on several key
factors: spatial and temporal variation in indicators, the strength of
relationships between indicators and responses (effect size), and
replication or sample size including number of sites, years, and plots.

Power analyses can employ standard methods for simple statistical
analyses or utilize simulations for more complex modeling approaches
(Johnson et al. 2015). These analyses require assumptions about spatial
and temporal variability of indicators and effect sizes specific to
individual studies and indicators.

**Temporal considerations and study design**

Increasing the number of years of data collection generally enhances
statistical power. Balanced designs with equal numbers of before and
after years provide greater statistical power than unbalanced designs
using the same total number of years (Braun et al. 2019). O\'Neal et al.
(2016) recommends collecting a minimum of two years of before-project
data, matched with two years of after-project data. While acquiring
pre-project data can be challenging, the statistical benefits of
balanced design make a compelling case for investing in before-project
data collection when feasible (Braun et al. 2019).

Within the NSB context, MPA sites experiencing greater
pre-implementation fishing intensity and other pressures may demonstrate
higher power to detect management-related changes compared to sites with
historically lower human activity levels.

**Before-After-Control-Impact (BACI) design**

BACI design represents one of the most appropriate methods for
evaluating management measure performance. This approach proves
particularly powerful because it controls for both temporal and spatial
variation, thereby improving the robustness of conclusions regarding
management effects. BACI design compares sampling periods before and
after measure implementation alongside impacted and control sites.

Successful BACI implementation requires suitable reference sites
(control sites) that remain fixed throughout the study period, while
within-site sampling units may be re-randomized or maintained as fixed
locations. External reference sites are highly recommended to optimize
conclusion scope and are required for BACI or similar sampling designs.
These sites should be positioned sufficiently distant from protected
areas to avoid edge effects, maintain comparable environmental
conditions and substrates, and exhibit similar historical pressure
levels (DFO 2021a).

**Reference sites and monitoring**

Areas currently under monitoring outside protected areas serve as
invaluable reference sites for assessing MPA performance and impact.
These monitored zones, often sharing similar ecological characteristics
with MPA areas, provide comparative benchmarks for evaluating changes
and patterns within protected regions (Nature United 2023). Through
examination of these external areas, scientists and conservationists can
establish meaningful parallels, contrasting impacts of human activities
and environmental changes in unprotected regions against conservation
outcomes within MPAs.

Reference areas facilitate understanding of natural variations,
human-induced pressures, and potential benefits derived from protective
measures. Analysis of differences and similarities enables assessment of
MPA efficacy, providing critical information for adaptive management and
conservation strategy refinement within protected marine environments.

Reference monitoring represents an emerging opportunity that utilizes
well-managed MPA sites as reference points for understanding global and
regional driver effects on ocean conditions (Fairweather 2012a;
Fairweather 2012b). Since reference sites will develop over time, this
approach has been identified as a low priority for the Network
monitoring framework, strategy, and associated plans (Network Monitoring
Framework). However, reference monitoring should be considered in
subsequent iterations of Network monitoring following sufficient
duration of site and Network establishment.

## Power analysis METHODOLOGY

Since 2003, Fisheries and Oceans Canada has conducted Hard Bottom
Longline (HBLL) surveys to monitor groundfish abundance and distribution
off the coast of BC. The survey targets inshore rockfish habitat,
specifically Yelloweye and Quillback rockfish habitat
\\cite{@doherty2019}. The HBLL survey consists of two survey series:
inside (HBLL INS, referring to waters between Vancouver Island and the
mainland) and the outside (HBLL OUT, all other BC waters). North and
south areas within each series are surveyed biennially. Three of the
four regions (HBLL OUT N, HBLL OUT S, and HBLL INS N) overlap with the
GBS MPA Network (Figure hbll-mpa-historical-overlay). The surveys use a
depth-stratified random sampling design, with a target allocation of 189
sets (HBLL OUT N), 252 (HBLL OUT S), and 70 (HBLL INS N).

We used a simulation-based power analysis to assess the ability of
existing monitoring programs to detect changes in population indices of
groundfish across the MPA Network. Our approach consisted of four steps:
(1) fit conditioning models to empirical data, (2) simulate population
recovery trends inside and outside of the MPAs under the assumption of
fishing cessation within MPAs, (3) apply two different sampling
strategies to the simulated population, and (4) test the power of these
sampling strategies to detect trends across the MPA Network by fitting
another spatiotemporal model to the combined historical and simulated
data.

Using a spatiotemporal modelling approach, we applied this power
analysis to five conservation priority species that are well sampled by
the HBLL survey: Yelloweye Rockfish, Quillback Rockfish, Lingcod,
Pacific Halibut, and Pacific Spiny Dogfish. This approach allows us to
test different scenarios, such as recovery trends within the MPA or
evaluation time frame, while incorporating some ecological complexity
and variability (Table label:scenario-summary). Power increases with
larger MPA effect sizes (e.g., faster recovery), higher abundances,
wider spatial distribution, more frequent sampling, and longer
evaluation times. Conversely, species with slower recovery rates, patchy
distributions, and/or lower abundance will require more intensive
sampling and longer evaluation time frames to detect population changes.

## POWER ANALYSIS RESULTS

Statistical power to detect MPA recovery trends varied across species
and effect sizes. For species with faster recovery rates, ≥80% power
could be reached within the first 10-15 years of MPA implementation
using status quo sampling, while for species with slower recovery it may
take 20-25 years of monitoring. Reducing MPA sampling frequency
generally delayed when ≥80% power was reached.

Helps us set expectations:

- At best expect detection of MPA effects in the best sampled species
  within 10-15 years

- Rates of recovery \~ 1% per year expect to detect effects in 20-25
  years

- Rates of recovery 2-3 % expect 10-15 years

- Rates \>4% expect within \<10 years

- Decreasing sampling within MPAs to every 4 years increased the number
  of years before we could detect an effect by \~ 5-10 years for a given
  recovery rate

Detection of significant effects before 10 years is likely to lead to
over estimates of effects 🡪 high exaggeration rates.

Stock assessment "no fishing" scenarios and life histories can help to
inform expectations of recovery rates
